title: ARTICLE ARCHIVE Leadership The Anatomy of Strategy
author: Nickhart
summary: Nickhart presents a worked example of a school improvement strategy architecture, beginning from foundational concepts -- schools as complex systems, problems as wicked, sense-making as dependent on adult ego development -- and building toward a cohesive hierarchy of actions at senior, subject, and year leader levels. Strategic intent is articulated through two metaphors: the horizon (improvement always receding) and the stream (upstream work on culture and curriculum is the mechanism; downstream data and intervention is necessary but not sufficient). Each leadership level has distinct but coordinated responsibilities across strategy, systems, culture, and capacity building. Psychological safety and aligned beliefs are non-negotiable cultural prerequisites -- improvement cannot happen without trust. The article also argues that informal learning is far more prevalent than formal CPD and that leaders should design for that reality. The article closes with a seven-point summary of what sound strategy requires.
points: - Strategic intent should be a narrative metaphor (the horizon, the stream) that is memorable and drives behaviour -- boxy priority lists with action columns fail to create the shared purpose that motivates distributed improvement. - The upstream/downstream stream metaphor is operationally useful: upstream work (culture, curriculum, expert teaching) builds sustainable improvement; downstream work (data, intervention) is necessary but not sufficient. - A cohesive hierarchy requires each level to have distinct but aligned responsibilities; when SLT and subject-leader plans are disconnected, accountability blurs and coherence collapses. - Truth does not rise to the top: leaders should assume colleagues are not showing them the actual lived reality and must be deliberately vigilant to behaviours that threaten trust. - Adult ego development per Gilbride's research with headteachers significantly shapes how leaders make sense of complex problems; supporting leaders to develop their ego is a prerequisite for better strategy, not a peripheral concern.
quotes: Designing the future before understanding the present can lead to misdiagnosing the school's needs and in turn misdirecting attention and resources. Understanding the present is not easy though.

We use the horizon as a metaphor for our school improvement work. The horizon is the furthest point that we can see, where the known meets the unknown, but horizons keep moving the closer we get. This is how we think about school improvement: no matter how good our provision, it can always be better.

Upstream is the deliberate crafting of culture and the experience of every child, colleague and parent; designing systems for knowledge building; a well designed curriculum; expert teaching; and succession planning.
Truth does not rise to the top. Whatever our own experiences of the school, they are unlikely to be the lived reality because our colleagues are likely to want to show us the best of themselves.

Trust takes years to build, seconds to break and forever to repair. How we respond to instances when behaviours threaten trust is crucial because trust is the lubricant for all school improvement work.
Informal learning is far more prevalent than formal learning and there are many more opportunities for us to influence learning than the regular, formal CPD sessions that we organise each week.
Formal and informal learning are neither binary nor dissociated from one another. Instead, they exist on a continuum where formal and informal learning are complementary and mutually reinforcing.
